podcast.title: Ricky Wilson's AIDS-Related Illness and Death (October 12, 1985)
podcast.body: Ricky Wilson, the guitarist for The B-52s, became the first notable musician to die from AIDS on October 12, 1985, just nine days after actor Rock Hudson's passing. He had been ill since 1983 and experienced severe health issues throughout most of 1985, including Kaposi's sarcoma, infections, and pneumonia. Due to the pervasive stigma associated with AIDS and gay men at the time, Wilson kept his condition private, with his sister and bandmate, Cindy Wilson, only learning of his diagnosis three days before his death. He passed away at Sloan Kettering Hospital in New York at the age of 32. "Ricky Wilson became the first notable musician to die of AIDS."

podcast.body: The B-52s formed in Athens, Georgia, after a cocktail gathering in a Chinese restaurant, with the intention of injecting silliness and fun into rock music, which they felt was too serious. podcast.title: The B-52s Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The American New Wave band The B-52s, prominent in the early 1980s, derived its name not from an aircraft but from the nickname for the voluminous beehive hairdos, known as "the B-52" in the 1960s, that were famously sported by the group's female vocalists, Cindy Wilson and Kate Pierson. "Their name comes from the nickname of the big B-hive hairdo's, sported by Cindy Wilson and Kate Pearson, the two women in the group."

xref.title: Death from Systemic Lupus (2022)
xref.body: In March 2018, Julee Cruise announced on Facebook that she was suffering from systemic lupus, experiencing severe pain and mobility issues, which led to a deep depression. She ultimately chose to end her life in a "controlled way" on June 9, 2022. Her husband reported that she passed away "on her own terms, no regrets, she is at peace," with The B-52s song "Rome" playing as she drifted off. "In March 2018, she announced on Facebook that she had systemic lupus and was living in a lot of pain. She found it hard to walk and stand, which sent her into a deep depression. And then she took her own life in a controlled way on June 9, 2022."

xref.title: Early Musical Influences
xref.body: His musical journey began with "Frankenstein" by the Edgar Winter Group, which ignited his passion for "big guitar rock." He then explored The Beatles, followed by Rush (given by a cousin), then Devo and Kiss (before B-52s and Devo). xref.title: Friends with Blondie and Ramones; Almost Signed to IRS; Influenced B-52s; Background Vocals on Blondie's Autoamerican
xref.body: The B-Girls formed in Toronto in 1977 with a sound closer to British Invasion mid-1960s than hard punk, though their look and attitude were fully punk. They toured with and opened for Teenage Head, the Viletones, and eventually The Clash, then relocated to New York where they became close with Blondie, the Ramones, the Cramps, and the Dead Boys. Members sang background vocals on Blondie's *Autoamerican* (1980), had demos produced by Debbie Harry and Mick Jones of The Clash, and nearly signed with IRS Records — which chose a Los Angeles band called the Go-Go's instead. The Go-Go's were fans of the B-Girls. The B-Girls' existence and sound also influenced a band from Georgia called the B-52s. No album was released before the original lineup fell apart by 1981. "This Canadian punk band influenced not just Blondie and the Go-Go's, but a band visiting New York from Georgia called the B-52s."

xref.body: Due to their overtly goofy and silly presentation, The B-52s were initially dismissed by some as merely a novelty band. "They were so goofy that some wrote them off as a novelty band, at least at first."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

xref.title: Inspiration for New Musicians
xref.body: Despite early skepticism, The B-52s, a mixed-gender and multi-sexual band, became a significant inspiration for a new generation of musicians, with Kurt Cobain notably transfixed by their performance on Saturday Night Live in 1980. "The truth is that this mixed gender and multi-sexual band became an inspiration for a new generation of musicians. Kurt Cobain saw the one Saturday Night Live in 1980. It was absolutely transfixed by them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

xref.title: Inspired by The B-52s
xref.body: Kurt Cobain was deeply inspired by The B-52s, stating he was "absolutely transfixed" after watching their performance on Saturday Night Live in 1980. "Kurt Cobain saw the one Saturday Night Live in 1980. It was absolutely transfixed by them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

xref.title: Music Video Pioneers (Early 1980s)
xref.body: The B-52s were grouped with Devo and other "left of center types" as bands that made for great music videos when the medium became popular in the early 1980s, due to their unique visual styles. "Divo was joined by the B-52s and a few other left of center types, all of whom made for great music videos when that became a thing in the early 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Notable Fan and Producer
xref.body: Fred Schneider of The B-52s is one of her biggest fans. He produced a couple of Christmas songs for her. "But one of her biggest fans is Fred Schneider of the B-52s. He produced a couple of Christmas songs for her."

srcs.episode: Still More Outsider Music

xref.title: Origin in Athens, Georgia
xref.body: R.E.M., considered the most successful band of its generation, originated from Athens, Georgia, a town of 70,000 people (20,000 of whom are University of Georgia students), located an hour east of Atlanta on Highway 78. The Athens music scene began in the mid-1970s with groups like The B-52s. "The most successful band of this generation came out of a town an hour east of Atlanta on Highway 78, just 70,000 people live there. And 20,000 of them are students at the University of Georgia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

xref.title: Post-Hit Career and Performances
xref.body: Despite "Falling" being her only true hit, Julee Cruise released several more albums and ventured into acting. She also toured extensively with The B-52s between 1992 and 1999, stepping in when regular member Cindy Wilson was unavailable, and made guest appearances on other artists' albums. "Alas, it was the only thing for Julie despite releasing several more albums. But that was okay because she got several acting gigs and toured with the B-52s when regular member Cindy Wilson was unavailable between 1992 and 1999."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest All-Time Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders: Part 1

xref.title: Quintessential American New Wave Band
xref.body: The B-52s are described as the quintessential American New Wave band, embodying the genre's spirit through their unique blend of catchy music, playful approach, and fashionably silly aesthetic. "B-52s were the only American quintessential new wave band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

xref.title: Rehearsal Location
xref.body: For an added touch of the surreal, The B-52s chose to rehearse in the blood-letting room of an abandoned mortuary, an unconventional choice that underscored their eccentric and offbeat artistic approach. "And for that surreal touch, the B-52s rehearsed in the blood-letting room of an abandoned mortuary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

xref.title: The B-52s Band Name Origin
xref.body: The American New Wave band The B-52s, prominent in the early 1980s, derived its name not from an aircraft but from the nickname for the voluminous beehive hairdos, known as "the B-52" in the 1960s, that were famously sported by the group's female vocalists, Cindy Wilson and Kate Pierson. "Their name comes from the nickname of the big B-hive hairdo's, sported by Cindy Wilson and Kate Pearson, the two women in the group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
